exports.1: We can lend you two people who spend every winter listening to ice shelves flex at frequencies nobody can hear, and the four low-frequency hydrophones they do it with. Give them a fortnight and a map of your water mains, and if it turns out to be a fridge they'll say so plainly and won't put it in a report.
exports.2: We'll send the woman who redrew our ferry timetable. She'll move one late service so it terminates in Northgate at eleven at night, because nobody has ever changed their mind about a suburb from a brochure -- they change it because they had to stand there twenty minutes and it was fine. Whatever you do, don't let anyone call it vibrant; that's how a place announces it's being sold to you.
exports.4: Send us your levels and we'll send back two diesel trash pumps, four hundred metres of lay-flat hose, and the bloke who cut the soak trenches under our own low corner. His rule is that water sitting for four days doesn't want draining, it wants somewhere better to be within a hundred metres -- so dig the low end on purpose, gravel the bottom, put reeds in it, and you've got a pond with a name instead of a puddle with a grudge.
exports.5: Be famous for something a person can eat standing up outside in bad weather with one hand. Ours is scallops in a thin curried white sauce inside short pastry, sold from a window, no seating and no tablecloth -- we'll send the pastry hand who's made them for thirty years and you can put your own fish in it.
exports.7: Plums won't wait, so stop trying to eat them. We'll put two truck-bed fruit presses and the crew who run our own March glut on a plane, plus a distiller whose entire philosophy is that fruit you can't sell is fruit you haven't got in a barrel yet -- pressed inside four days, in cask by Sunday, and it becomes next year's problem instead of this week's.
exports.8: Nine hundred metres of the slatted windbreak we use along the wharf, and the only thing you need to know about it: it's half gaps. Solid walls don't stop wind, they just hand it back to you faster twenty metres on. And give up on awnings -- string wire between the lamp posts instead and let the avenue dry the town's washing, since it's going to do it anyway.
exports.11: Seven hundred seedlings out of our foreshore nursery -- she-oak, boobialla, coastal tea-tree -- all three already growing in sand that takes a face full of salt spray twice a day, and none of them needing a stake after the first year. Plant them closer together than looks sensible; the front row is meant to die for the rest, and the she-oaks make a noise in the wind you can claim you intended.
exports.12: We run a night room off the back of the hospital laundry: ten till seven, cots rather than activities, one adult to four children, and a minibus at both ends. The thing you're actually short of isn't carers, it's a licence category that exists after six in the evening -- we'll send the two pages of ours you can copy word for word, and the woman who wrote them, for a fortnight.
exports.13: We'll do it. Our lot have never once been described as cordial on a field, we'll travel, and we'll take the same weekend every year -- home and away, and the trophy has to be an ugly object with a bad story attached, not a cup. Fair warning: nobody stays polite about us for long, which is what you said you wanted.
exports.14: Send us photographs of the trusses and we'll send three shipwrights. A roof is a hull upside down, and scarfing new timber into an old frame while the thing stays in use is the only job they've ever had -- fixed price agreed before the first cut, which will do more for your permits than the scaffolding ever did.
exports.15: A window, not a room. Ours opens at four and shuts at eight: one pot of something brothy, bread, black tea in a heavy cup, no music and no daylight bulbs, because people coming off a night don't want waking up, they want letting down gently. We'll send the urn, the soup, and the two women who run it, on the condition nobody calls it a concept.

answers.1: Camping. I went to considerable trouble to own a house with a roof on it, and the proposal is that I go and sleep outside on purpose.
answers.2: On a boat, whatever the sky's doing. You learn the shape of a place from the water in twenty minutes and it saves an hour of explaining -- then chips off the punt, standing up, and if it's raining that's part of it.
answers.3: That something I signed off on eleven years ago is still working, and the person telling me had forgotten it was ever a decision anyone made.
answers.5: A metre of the eight-strand off the ferry cleats, spliced properly by hand, so whoever opens it knows somebody here could still do that.
answers.7: Home before the light goes. I cook what I cook most Tuesdays -- a piece of fish, potatoes, more butter than is defensible -- with the coastal waters forecast on, which my wife calls a hobby and I call due diligence. Then an hour in the shed re-whipping the ends of whatever rope has gone furry, which produces nothing anyone needs. Bed by half nine. That's the whole thing and I'm not embarrassed about it.
answers.8: Bev, in the works depot. My predecessor left me a handover folder; Bev went through it and told me which parts of it had never once been true.
answers.10: Another port. I couldn't live somewhere the water doesn't do anything -- somewhere small and wet with a working wharf and a hill behind it, and I'd be complaining about their ferries inside a fortnight.
answers.12: Whichever one is easier to undo. If they're both easy to undo, whichever one the person who has to maintain it would rather maintain.
answers.13: The back porch, which was really a laundry with ambitions. Louvre windows on two sides that never properly shut, so it sat at outside temperature plus about two degrees, and it always smelled of wet wool because the drying rack hung over the trough. There was a chest freezer along one wall with a flat cushion on it and that was my chair -- I did my homework there because after seven nobody walked through. Dad's boots by the door, always facing out so you could step straight into them. I'd know that room in the dark.
answers.14: The early ferry, upper deck, outside, in weather. Nobody follows you out there and nobody can talk over the engine.
answers.15: The bell on the ferry ramp. Two clangs: means we're going whether you're aboard or not.
answers.16: The key to a boatshed that was pulled down in 2003. It's still on my ring. It opens nothing, it weighs nothing, and I'm not doing anything about it.
